column2: ILD (usually NSIP) affects most patients with systemic sclerosis, especially anti-Scl-70, and is the leading cause of death; PAH is the other lung complication.
In a retired boilermaker with clubbing and crackles, HRCT best confirms asbestosis (basal reticulation with pleural plaques) and screens for cancer.
Fever, dry cough, hypoxaemia and new diffuse infiltrates within months of methotrexate is methotrexate pneumonitis: stop it, exclude infection, give steroids.
Proximal weakness with high CK and ESR is polymyositis, complicated by ILD in up to 40% (anti-Jo-1); screen for malignancy.
Multiple smooth nodules stable for 5 years in long-standing seropositive RA are rheumatoid (necrobiotic) nodules.
Sarcoid-like granulomatous disease with BHL after occupational exposure is berylliosis; beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test confirms.
Diffuse ground-glass with centrilobular nodules and a pet parrot is hypersensitivity pneumonitis (bird fancier's lung); avoid the antigen.
Organising pneumonia unresponsive to antibiotics responds rapidly to prednisolone ~0.75–1 mg/kg tapered over 6–12 months.
Symptoms 4–8 h after mouldy hay in a barn are acute farmer's lung, so his occupation is the cause.
EAA: avoid the antigen; corticosteroids speed recovery in severe or progressive disease. It is immune-mediated, not infective.
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis causes upper/mid-zone fibrosis with restriction and low TLCO; avian precipitins support it.
The commonest ECG finding in PE is sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 and RBBB are uncommon.
Pleuritic pain and breathlessness with calf pain 3 weeks after surgery is PE: Wells score, CTPA and anticoagulate meanwhile.
Two-level Wells ≥ 4.5 (PE likely): go straight to CTPA with interim anticoagulation; D-dimer only rules out unlikely PE.
Sudden breathlessness, haemoptysis, cyanosis and raised JVP in pregnancy is PE with RV strain; treat with LMWH (no DOAC/warfarin).
Massive PE causes collapse, hypoxaemia and RV failure; pleuritic pain and haemoptysis come from infarction by smaller distal emboli.
Raised JVP and leg oedema in COPD are cor pulmonale (hypoxic pulmonary hypertension); LTOT improves survival.
RV hypertrophy in cor pulmonale gives a left parasternal heave, loud P2 and functional TR.
Bosentan (endothelin receptor antagonist) treats PAH; others are PDE-5 inhibitors, riociguat and prostacyclin agents. Monitor LFTs.
Raised JVP with pruned peripheral vessels suggests pulmonary hypertension; transthoracic echo is the first test, then RHC.
PAH is vascular, so volumes, spirometry and muscle strength are normal; the typical abnormality is an isolated low DLCO.
RV dysfunction in PAH recovers after bilateral lung transplantation as afterload falls; heart–lung only for complex disease.
In idiopathic PAH, perform acute vasoreactivity testing at RHC; the ~10% responders get high-dose CCBs, others combination PAH therapy.
Pulmonary hypertension with clear lungs, normal perfusion scan and prior appetite suppressants is drug-induced PAH; confirm by RHC.
Cor pulmonale with normal lung fields and spirometry suggests CTEPH from recurrent small emboli; V/Q scan, endarterectomy may cure.
Haemoptysis, clubbing and localised wheeze with a mass in a 70-year-old is bronchial carcinoma: bronchoscopy and biopsy (± EBUS).
Stony dullness with absent breath sounds and a central trachea is a pleural effusion, likely malignant; aspirate for cytology.
Na⁺ 104 with seizure in lung cancer is SIADH (small cell); give hypertonic saline boluses, raising Na⁺ ≤ 8–10 mmol/L in 24 h.
Lung cancer risks: smoking, radon, asbestos, metals (chromium, nickel, arsenic), pollution, radiotherapy. Lead is not a carcinogen here.
Effusion in suspected lung cancer: ultrasound-guided aspiration for cytology diagnoses and stages (M1a) and relieves breathlessness.
Dermatomyositis is a paraneoplastic skin manifestation of lung cancer; screen adults presenting with it.
Haemoptysis, weight loss, clubbing and localised wheeze with an opacity in a heavy smoker is bronchogenic carcinoma; urgent CT and tissue.
Cushingoid features in a smoker with lung cancer are ectopic ACTH (small cell or carcinoid); often hypokalaemic alkalosis dominates.
High-dose dexamethasone suppresses pituitary (Cushing disease) but not usually ectopic ACTH; petrosal sinus sampling is more reliable.
Hyponatraemia with normal K⁺ and concentrated urine in lung cancer is SIADH; fluid restriction, treat tumour, tolvaptan if refractory.
A central tumour occluding a bronchus causes collapse: opacification with volume loss and the mediastinum pulled towards it.
TNM stage at diagnosis is the strongest prognostic factor (stage IA ~70–90% vs stage IV < 10% 5-year survival).
Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causes hoarseness and bovine cough, not breathlessness.
Whole-hemithorax dullness with the trachea pulled towards it is lung collapse from an obstructing tumour; an effusion pushes it away.
A thick-walled cavitating mass in a smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss is most likely cavitating squamous carcinoma.
A widened mediastinum with inflammation in a young woman suggests lymphoma; contrast CT chest, abdomen, pelvis to stage and find biopsy sites.
A spiculated solid upper-lobe nodule ≥ 8 mm in a smoker (Brock risk > 10%) needs PET-CT next (BTS).
An FDG-avid nodule without nodal or distant uptake in a fit patient is presumed stage I: lobectomy (SABR if unfit).
PET-CT shows uptake in the right upper lobe primary and right hilar node (N1); sample PET-positive nodes (EBUS) before deciding.
EBUS-TBNA of PET-avid hilar nodes gives diagnosis and stage in one low-risk procedure (NICE NG122).
Persistent dull chest wall pain with effusion decades after asbestos exposure is mesothelioma; CT and pleural biopsy.
Upper-lobe location raises nodule malignancy risk (Brock), as do age, female sex, emphysema, size, spiculation and part-solid nature.
